classificationNotes: Source-draft Mummies are treated as ritually preserved, linen-wrapped dead whose grave goods and offices supply authored encounter ranks, not as a biological people or evidence about any real culture, religion, ethnicity, divinity, royal legitimacy, morality, or afterlife. Sand and dust are family-native burial residue and non-affinity staging; true affinities require separate material and behavior construction.
visualConstants: A stiff-limbed human or humanoid silhouette remains wrapped from head to foot, with arms held forward, crossed, guarding, inscribing, or commanding through readable linen tension.
Sun-bleached linen, sand beige, desert ochre, deep gold, lapis blue, and turquoise remain funerary materials and symbols rather than affinity colors.
Linen bandage, dried flesh, gold leaf, lapis, carnelian, bronze, and sandstone grave goods stay materially distinct and retain visible knots, stitches, glyph routes, and breakable seals.
Family-native sand and dust follow disturbed wrappings, tomb movement, and burial objects without becoming Earth or Wind affinity by themselves.
Escalation adds precious thread, glyph density, collars, masks, armor, headdresses, and sarcophagus regalia while the bandages never come off and always explain binding and counterplay.
escalationAxis: Crude wrapping knots become bronze guard bindings, processional glyph circuits, a masked tomb formation, and a royal sarcophagus engine whose dismantled cartouches remove commands and unwrap a simpler final phase.

constructionDimensions: Family-native, non-affinity materials remain dry linen, desiccated flesh, bronze, gold leaf, lapis, carnelian, turquoise, sandstone grave goods, burial dust, and ordinary tomb sand with visible age and craft.

Motion and effects stay funerary and mechanical: bandages tighten, knots turn, charms strike linen, glyph ink conducts faint ritual light, dust shakes from folds, and sand moves only when a wrapped foot, mask, weapon, or sarcophagus displaces it.
normal.counterplaySignal: Loose end knots, bronze stitches, interrupted glyphs, mask straps, cartouche seals, sarcophagus hinges, and exposed dried flesh preserve every established weak point.
forbidden: unexplained elemental anatomy
unexplained elemental glow
unexplained environmental wake
Treating family-native sand, dust, sandstone, faint glyph light, or gold alone as an elemental affinity

constructionDimensions: Wrappings become a controlled funerary kiln through char-edged linen layers, ceramic scarab vents, heat-darkened gold stitches, ember channels beneath rather than replacing bandages, and brazier fittings on mask or sarcophagus hardware.
Actions follow a heat-and-cool bind cycle: selected glyph strips tighten under heat, vents open, smoke follows the moving wrap, and a linen knot or metal fitting cools visibly after commitment.
fire.counterplaySignal: The ceramic scarab vent opens and the active gold stitch darkens after a heated bind; striking that cooling stitch releases the wrapped limb or command seal.
forbidden: Palette-only fire treatment without kiln materials, vent hardware, and heat-tightened wrapping
Glow-only fire treatment without an ember route or cooling stitch
Burning away the bandages that define the family and its counterplay
Generic flames or orange sand that conceal knots, glyphs, charms, and dried anatomy

constructionDimensions: Earth affinity is distinguished from ordinary tomb sand by structural mineralization: compressed sandstone splints under linen, load-bearing lapis joints, crystal scarab clasps, and carved stone channels on masks, armor, or sarcophagus lids.
Stance and attacks become masonry-driven through keyed foot sockets, settling plates, pale fractures at wrapped joints, and localized blocks rising only along a visible carved channel.
earth.counterplaySignal: A load-bearing lapis clasp or sandstone splint turns chalk-white after a committed step or bind; breaking it releases the linen tension and collapses the connected structure.
forbidden: Palette-only earth treatment or extra tan sand without structural mineralization and changed load paths
Glow-only earth treatment without a fracture, clasp, or masonry joint
Pasted rocks that hide wrapping logic, glyphs, masks, or human silhouette
Ordinary family-native tomb dust mislabeled as Earth affinity

constructionDimensions: Bandages become directional pressure craft through vane-folded loose ends, hollow bronze charms, sail-stiff collars, perforated masks, and headdress or sarcophagus fins that preserve full wrapping coverage.
Motion reveals force direction through taut strip lines, whistling charm rows, dust streamlines limited to contact, and a still controlling knot, glyph, mask strap, or cartouche seal.
wind.counterplaySignal: Loose ends pull into one direction while the controlling knot or cartouche becomes perfectly still; entering the lee or cutting that anchor collapses the pressure-driven wrap.
forbidden: Palette-only wind treatment without vane folds, hollow charms, and directional wrapping behavior
Glow-only wind treatment without a still anchor or readable pressure direction
A generic sandstorm that duplicates family-native tomb dust and hides the Mummy
Free-floating bandages that detach from the binding route or expose the whole corpse

constructionDimensions: Preservation becomes hydraulic through resin-dark wet linen, sealed alabaster reservoirs, shell or silver valves, fluid-filled glyph channels, and pressure bladders fitted beneath collars, armor, and sarcophagus hardware.
Actions show coherent filling and drainage through tightening saturated wraps, wet reflection, narrow jets along glyph paths, lifted valves, and slackening linen when pressure is lost.
water.counterplaySignal: An alabaster reservoir fills toward the active limb or seal and its valve rises; opening it drains that route and exposes the underlying knot or dried joint.
forbidden: Palette-only water treatment without saturated materials, reservoirs, and pressure behavior
Glow-only water treatment without coherent channels, valves, and drainage
Shapeless blue wrapping or a liquid corpse that erases linen construction
Mist or spray that conceals glyph order, knots, mask straps, or sarcophagus tells

forms.battlefieldDuty: Probe footwork by dragging one crude wrapping end behind a stiff advance, then pulling the strip into a short ankle snare before the exposed knot can be retied.
forms.teachingGoal: Teach that linen is both animation and weakness: avoid the visible strip, step on it after the pull, and attack the knot while dried flesh shows through the loosened gap.
forms.signatureMechanic: Common-Grave Draw: the Husk advances on one dragging leg while a grey bandage end trails from its hip; when the arms lift, the end loops around the nearest ankle line and retracts toward the hip knot.
forms.telegraph: Empty eye holes face down, both stiff arms rise, and the dirty trailing strip straightens from the dragging leg to its hip knot.
forms.counterplay: Step over or pin the strip before it retracts, then cut the visible hip knot; the Husk must stop and rewrap the gap before it can snare again.
forms.visualDelta: A dried human husk in crude grey head-to-foot bandages, one dragging leg, empty eye holes, exposed flesh in several gaps, and one extra-long loose strip tied at the hip.

forms.battlefieldDuty: Hold a repeatable doorway or relic line by crossing khopesh and wrapped forearm, transferring the block through a row of bronze charms that leaves one stitch overloaded.
forms.teachingGoal: Teach mature binding: do not batter the dry front; draw the committed guard, read which charm row tightens, and cut the last loaded stitch from the side.
forms.signatureMechanic: Tomb Cross: the Guard crosses its bronze khopesh over one wrapped forearm and turns sideways across a threshold. Bronze charms stitched from wrist to shoulder carry the impact, but the topmost charm pulls one linen seam fully open after the block.
forms.telegraph: The simple headcloth settles, khopesh and forearm cross, and bronze charms click in order from wrist toward shoulder until the final stitch shines.
forms.counterplay: Bait the cross with a light attack, move around the weapon side, and cut the final shoulder stitch before the charm row relaxes.
forms.visualDelta: A taut, dry, fully wrapped guard with a simple headcloth, bronze scarab charms sewn in ordered rows, and a bronze khopesh whose curve matches the crossed-arm stance.
forms.lowerFormInteraction: Husks can drag loose ends behind the guarded threshold, but breaking the Tomb Cross's final stitch opens the line and tears any Husk strip caught beneath its stance.

forms.battlefieldDuty: Qualitatively pivot the encounter into ordered route control by unspooling three gilded glyph bands that record movement and then rewind along the same processional sequence.
forms.teachingGoal: Teach players to read glyph order, deliberately cross one strip to create an escape break, and interrupt the collar clasp before the recorded path pulls combatants backward.
forms.signatureMechanic: Written Procession: the Servant extends three gilded bands from its jeweled collar, touching floor points in a clearly numbered glyph order. After the third point, the bands tighten in reverse and drag anyone standing on a recorded segment back toward the previous point. Crossing two bands before completion tangles them; striking the open collar clasp cancels the rewind.
forms.telegraph: The jeweled collar opens at one front clasp, faint family-native glyph light travels one-two-three along separate bands, and the Servant's stiff hands cross before the order reverses.
forms.counterplay: Track the numbered glow, leave the latest segment, cross two loose bands to tangle them, or strike the exposed collar clasp before the hands complete their cross.
forms.visualDelta: A fully wrapped ritual attendant with gilded bands layered over linen, a jeweled pectoral collar with an opening front clasp, and three long glyph-inscribed strips controlled by stiff fingers.
forms.lowerFormInteraction: Husks and Tomb Guards are pulled backward along the same recorded sequence to renew snares or thresholds; tangling the bands displaces those lower forms and interrupts every rewind.

forms.battlefieldDuty: Assemble lower Mummies into a four-sided tomb formation by turning its gold death-mask toward one side and directing native sand only as a readable footprint record.
forms.teachingGoal: Teach formation rotation: the mask faces the protected side, the rear strap and ceremonial armor seam carry its weight, and breaking that seam permanently removes one formation wall.
forms.signatureMechanic: Four-Faced Tomb: the Champion's full death-mask turns toward a cardinal side while ceremonial armor plates unfold along that edge. Husks trail snare strips across one flank, Tomb Guards cross the front, and a Sacred Servant writes a return path behind. Sand disturbed at their feet records every occupied line but has no independent elemental force. The opposite mask strap stretches visibly under the formation load.
forms.telegraph: The gold mask rotates with a dry click, one armor edge opens, native sand swirls only around moving feet, and the opposite linen strap pulls away from the wrapped skull.
forms.counterplay: Move through the side before the armor edge closes, avoid the familiar lower-form lines, and cut the rear mask strap; each broken strap prevents the Champion from rebuilding that side.
forms.visualDelta: A fully wrapped elite in ceremonial armor with a complete gold death-mask, four visible retaining straps, a broad collar, and family-native tomb sand circling only its stiff footwork.
forms.lowerFormInteraction: Husks supply snare flanks, Tomb Guards hold the faced edge, and Sacred Servants inscribe the rear return route; breaking the corresponding mask strap opens all three duties on that side.

forms.battlefieldDuty: Command a royal tomb boss through a floating sarcophagus lid and four cartouche rails that bind, guard, rewind, and form lower Mummies before each broken rail simplifies the arena and final wrapped body.
forms.teachingGoal: Test mastery of loose knots, loaded charm stitches, glyph order, and mask formations while teaching that the source title does not imply invulnerability: every royal command depends on a breakable material seal.
forms.signatureMechanic: Royal Passage: the sarcophagus lid floats behind the God-King like a banner on four linen-and-gold rails. The Knot cartouche pulls Husks from common-grave alcoves; the Bronze cartouche equips survivors as Tomb Guards; the Script cartouche lets a Sacred Servant record a three-point procession; and the Mask cartouche closes a Pharaoh's Champion formation. The towering headdress points to one cartouche while family-native sand follows the moving rail, never acting independently. Cutting the lit cartouche's linen hinge permanently drops that lid quarter and removes its command. After two quarters fall, the God-King steps out of the remaining frame; its headdress shortens with each lost rail and it cycles only surviving rites around exposed wrapping knots.
forms.telegraph: One lapis headdress vane aligns with a cartouche, its gold glyph becomes faintly readable, the matching lid rail swings forward, and lower Mummies cross their arms in the selected learned posture.
forms.counterplay: Read the named cartouche and lower-form tell, disrupt the required Mummy or route, then cut the exposed linen hinge while the rail is forward; every dropped lid quarter removes one rite, clears an arena lane, and exposes another royal wrapping knot.
forms.visualDelta: A fully wrapped royal dead figure in towering gold-and-lapis headdress and regalia, framed by a sarcophagus lid divided into four cartouche quarters and a permanent sandstorm halo of family-native, non-affinity burial sand rather than Earth or Wind affinity; the halo stays bounded to the royal silhouette and readable rails.
forms.lowerFormInteraction: The four cartouches produce or command Husks, Tomb Guards, Sacred Servants, and a Pharaoh's Champion; each severed hinge permanently ends that lower-form rite and simplifies the God-King's remaining phase.
